text: A family hires a maid partly to keep her out of a brothel, then has to live with what they have taken in. The setting is the Deep South of the 1930s, and the Hillyers consider themselves decent people; charity is the frame they put around Rose, and it keeps slipping. She knows exactly what her presence does to men, which the household treats as her defect rather than its own. Martha Coolidge films this as a domestic comedy that keeps sobering up. Much of it is watching: a wife's patience, a husband's stiffening propriety, a boy learning what adults do with a rule they will not say aloud. The Academy gave the film two acting prizes, both of them to women, which is the correct accounting - the drama sits in their faces while the men do the talking.

Montauban, 1944: a surgeon decides the countryside is safer than the town and sends his wife and daughter ahead to an old family castle. Julien Dandieu goes on operating in the hospital while the German army settles into the streets outside it. A week later he drives out for the weekend. Robert Enrico shoots that journey as a slow arrival at information the traveller does not yet have, and films the summer country as though the war had declined to touch it. The picture was made three decades after the occupation it describes, close enough to be speaking to people who remembered the streets in it. It took the Cesar for direction. Dandieu is not a symbol of anything. He is a man good with his hands, and the film keeps its eye on those hands.

A journalist whose copy nobody wants and a businessman who will not name his business find each other in Nicaragua. They stay together longer than either intended. Claire Denis gives this 138 minutes, roughly fifty more than a thriller would want, and the surplus is the argument: the film runs on waiting, heat, unpaid bills, drinks bought with somebody else's money, the daily arithmetic of people who cannot simply book a flight out. Sex here is a transaction and also not one. The conspiracy stays offscreen, sensed in the manner of men at the next table and in which official happens to be available today. It carries a Grand Prix and divides its audience, and the division declares itself early - anyone waiting for the plot to accelerate will spend two hours at odds with the film.

The mannered French of a Marivaux comedy, spoken by teenagers on a housing estate outside Paris at the volume and in the accent they actually use: that collision is the engine. Krimo wants nothing to do with the school play until Lydia is cast, at which point he takes the lead role so that he can stand near her and say words about love that someone else wrote for other mouths. Abdellatif Kechiche shoots close and lets scenes run past their point - overlapping argument, mockery that doubles as affection, kids talking each other into corners and refusing to climb out. Two hours and four minutes, most of it rehearsal. The Cesar for best film went to a picture that never settles whether the borrowed language is helping Krimo or exposing him.

Jean takes whoever he wants and calls it freedom, until Laura arrives and the arrangement starts to cost. Cyril Collard's film, made in France in 1992, has the nerve to refuse to make Jean likeable on the way to making him legible: he is easy company, careless, and unkind by turns to Laura and to Samy, who are less rivals than people held in reserve. Two hours and six minutes with someone this evasive is a demand, and the length is doing work, because desire here is repetitive and the crisis it circles cannot be settled by choosing one of them. Collard keeps Jean in nearly every scene, so the judgement of him has to be made by the viewer rather than handed over. The Cesar for best film went to it. No confession, no lesson, nobody absolved.

Seventy-nine minutes, and the film is over before most dramas have finished setting the table. Fatima was born in Algeria and lives in France with two teenage daughters who have grown up inside a language she handles less readily than they do; the distance between the three of them is measured out in ordinary sentences that fail to arrive. Philippe Faucon works close and small - kitchen, corridor, the negotiations of a household - and lets the daughters be difficult without turning them into ingrates. The performance at the centre took a Cesar, and the brevity is pressure rather than modesty: nothing here is permitted to become a speech. Women like Fatima usually turn up in films as somebody else's mother, explained by the person doing the explaining. Not here.

A bank with a hole in its accounts needs one negligent employee, and it finds him upstairs, in a good office. Henri Rainier has the wife, the daughters, the salary; he is summoned, accused, and out of a job before he has grasped what was decided about him. What follows is an investigation conducted in offices and corridors, moving toward the discovery that the fault was assigned before the meeting began. Christian de Chalonge keeps the temperature low. The threat is procedural, delivered by courteous men under no obligation to find Rainier interesting. A hundred and five minutes of conversation across desks, in which the danger is audible mainly in the tone people use when they already know how a thing will end.

The fix is not to deny the scandal but to manufacture a war, and to hire a Hollywood producer to build it. With the vote weeks away and the President accused of sexual misconduct, the job passes to people who think in terms of coverage rather than truth, and the film then follows the work the way it would follow any production: the pitch, the personnel, the deadline. Barry Levinson plays it as a comedy of craft, which is the cruel choice - the pleasure on offer is watching competent people solve problems that happen to be crimes. Ninety-seven minutes, and quick about it. It took a Silver Bear. What has dated least is the tone: nobody involved is troubled, and the job keeps being satisfying to them.

A woman is teaching French in Seoul, and her method consists largely of asking students what they actually felt while they were speaking. Iris has come from elsewhere and works without much apparent system; the film gives her four encounters across a single day, and each turns into an interrogation conducted in the friendliest available register - about a poem, about a family history, about the opinion a person privately holds of themselves. Hong Sang-soo keeps to ninety minutes and to conversation. Repetition is the technique rather than a shortage of material: the second exchange rhymes with the first, and the rhyme is where the comedy sits. It carried a Silver Bear out of Berlin. Whether Iris is wise or simply at a loose end goes unsettled, and she is untroubled by the question.

A deaf child in London becomes the ground on which her parents fight. Mandy is mute through most of her early childhood, and by the time she reaches school age the family is close to breaking up: Christine, her mother, has heard of a residential school where deaf children are taught to speak, and the question of sending her away divides the house. Alexander Mackendrick, filming in the early 1950s, gives the household tempers and closed doors and gives the school methods rather than miracles. Much of the picture is adults deciding on behalf of someone who cannot yet argue back. It took the Grand Jury Prize at Venice. The best of it stays at child height, where the arguments of grown people arrive like weather and the world is a set of moving mouths.
